title: Eye anatomy (cutaway)
claims: Light path: cornea → aqueous (anterior chamber) → pupil → lens → vitreous → retina (macula/fovea for central vision).
Aqueous is made by the ciliary body, passes through the pupil, and drains through the trabecular meshwork / canal of Schlemm at the iridocorneal angle.
Acute angle-closure: the peripheral iris bows forward against the trabecular meshwork, blocking aqueous drainage and causing a rapid IOP rise.
Angle-closure presents with painful red eye, halos, headache, nausea/vomiting, mid-dilated fixed pupil and hazy cornea. It is an emergency.
Angle-closure treatment: lower IOP (acetazolamide, topical beta-blocker, alpha agonist, pilocarpine once IOP falls) then laser peripheral iridotomy. Avoid mydriatics.
Rhegmatogenous (most common) retinal detachment: fluid passes through a tear and separates the neurosensory retina from the pigment epithelium/choroid.
Retinal detachment presents with flashes, new floaters, then a "curtain" over part of the visual field; painless.
Retinal detachment is an emergency: laser/cryo for tears; pneumatic retinopexy, scleral buckle or vitrectomy for detachment.
Central retinal artery occlusion: sudden, painless monocular vision loss.
In CRAO the retina turns pale (ischemic) while the fovea stays red (cherry-red spot), because the fovea is supplied by the choroid.
CRAO has an embolic source (carotid, heart); consider giant cell arteritis. Ocular emergency.
